Home backup · US 120 V

Best power station for a portable air conditioner

Every machine below is ranked by a calculation, not by an opinion, and on this load the calculation returns nothing: not one published US record clears a floor-standing portable air conditioner outright. The largest machine here is a tight fit and the other eleven cannot start it at all. That is the finding on this page rather than a caveat to it.

Not one record in this region’s library clears this set outright — the closest anything gets is a tight fit (1 of 12), and a buy button belongs on a clear pass, not a tight one. The rows below carry the full working for each.

What would change this

What changes this answer is not a bigger battery — it is a different air conditioner. Every refusal on this page traces to one instant, the moment a fixed-speed compressor is thrown across the line, and that instant is a property of the appliance rather than of the machine feeding it. A variable-speed unit has no such instant: its own drive board ramps the compressor up, we have found no start-up current published for it because there is no such instant to measure, and this site ranks those separately — on that page most records clear the load rather than almost none. It is a different purchase, not a workaround, and the page says plainly what it can and cannot prove about duration. See the variable-speed ranking

The rule is written out under the list, the load is itemised with its figure’s source, and every row links to the calculator with that machine and this air conditioner already filled in — so you can re-run any number on this page yourself.

How this list is ordered

Four gates, applied in this order to every published US record. There is no score and no weighting — each gate either separates two machines or hands them to the next one.

  1. 1 Does it run the set?

    Every record is put through the compatibility engine against all of the loads at once — running watts against continuous output, the worst start-up instant against the surge ceiling, waveform where a load demands one. Green first, then the tight fits, then anything the engine could not read, then the machines that cannot do it. A machine that cannot start the load in front of it is not a cheaper option.

  2. 2 Can we prove how long?

    A runtime is only printed where the brand publishes what it takes to compute one — a usable-capacity coefficient, whether stated as depth of discharge and inverter efficiency or as one combined figure — and never from the number on the box. Records that reach the target sort first, records with a proven but shorter figure next (longest first: inside that band none of them does the job, so the one that gets closest wins), and records whose duration cannot be proven at all sort last inside their verdict band. That is a statement about published data, not about the hardware, and each of those rows says so.

  3. 3 Can it be bought today?

    A record under a verified out-of-stock policy, or one we may not sell into your state, sorts behind an equivalent one that can be bought. It stays on the list with the reason attached rather than disappearing. Whether WattPair happens to hold a purchase link for a record is not part of this gate and never moves it: a machine we cannot link to is ranked exactly as if we could, and simply carries no buy button.

  4. 4 Then price.

    Cheapest first, inside everything above. One mains standard and one currency per page, so every comparison is like for like. A record with no verified price sorts to the back of its own band — the absence of a price is not a low price.

The loads this ranks against

One 14,000 BTU dual-hose portable air conditioner, on its own, at 1,300 W. Two things about that record matter more than the number. Its start-up figure is 6,900 VA, taken from the data sheet of the rotary compressor inside it rather than from the appliance nameplate — plug-in room air conditioners are certified to a standard that does not require a locked-rotor rating on the label at all, so one level down is the only place the figure exists. And it is the same compressor-class figure the fixed-speed window-unit page ranks against, meeting a running draw about half again as large: that is why this page ends with nothing recommended where that one ends with one machine. This library also holds no usable power data for SINGLE-hose units, which are the cheaper and more common kind, and it will not extrapolate to them — a single-hose unit exhausts indoor air outdoors and pulls unconditioned air back in through every gap in the room, so its real-world efficiency is worse in a way its wattage does not show.

The finding is at the first gate, not the second: nothing here starts the load, so no duration is reached that any target could be compared against. The duty cycle behind the energy figure is the continuous-use curve rather than the seasonal average a government test procedure publishes for residential use, because an outage or a heat wave is when the thing runs all day, and the seasonal figure would understate the energy roughly fivefold.

Why 1 record carries no printable runtime

1 of the 12 records here starts and holds this load set and still carries no runtime this page will print, for one reason: we have found no depth of discharge and no inverter efficiency published by EcoFlow for it, so the hours a reader actually wants cannot be computed from anything but the number on the box — and dividing a nameplate by a load is the one thing this site will not do. The other side of that is BLUETTI and Jackery: they are the only brands here that publish both, which is the whole reason every proven runtime above belongs to them. The rule rewarded disclosure, not hardware.

What their rows do carry is the bound: that record’s nameplate over this set’s average draw of 1,170 W, which is arithmetic anyone can redo against the summary above — floored, never rounded up, so the printed ceiling never claims an hour more than the number supports — and it is printed on every one of those rows. But it is a ceiling and not a duration: it assumes the pack surrenders every watt-hour printed on it and that the inverter loses nothing turning DC into AC, and no battery does either. The real hours sit somewhere below that ceiling, and the two missing figures are exactly what would say how far below. That is the difference between a number this page will print and a number it will not.

The scope of that finding, stated: as of 2026-08-08 we read each manufacturer’s own published documents for these 1 models and found no depth-of-discharge and no inverter-efficiency figure in them. It is a statement about what those documents contained on that date — not a claim that the number exists nowhere. Send us one that is published and the record moves, and the row moves with it. Two counts are in play on this page and both are right: for 5 of the 12 records in this pool we have found neither figure published, which is the number the summary above is the other side of, and the 1 named here is the one that got far enough up the ranking for it to cost it a position. This is a statement about published data, not about the hardware — the verdict column judges that separately, and it comes first.

The load that changes the answer

Add a full-size refrigerator to the same set and the first gate, which was already refusing every record here, goes on refusing them: not one of the 12 clears it outright — 1 is a tight fit and 11 cannot do it at all. The reason is one instant: a full-size refrigerator asks for 286 W at start-up on its own — 5.2× its own running draw, against 7,800 W for everything on the list above put together. That start-up figure is a category envelope: we have found no published start-up rating for this unit itself. There is no “before” to contrast against here — nothing on this page clears the air conditioner on its own, so nothing can be taken away from it by a refrigerator. What would move this list is a different air conditioner, not a smaller set. The quiz carries this set as a preset.

Questions people ask about this list

How many of the 12 actually run it?
0 of 12 do, and the other 12 are the finding on this page. 1,300 W of running draw and 7,800 W at the worst start-up instant is what every published US record is measured against, and 11 of 12 are refused outright — on surge ceiling and continuous output; 1 clears it only as a tight fit on surge ceiling. Which means the buying question splits in two: whether a given machine starts it at all, and only then how long it holds. The ranked list above answers them in that order.
Is a 14,000 BTU portable unit really 14,000 BTU?
Not under the rating that governs sizing. The same manufacturer page carries two capacity figures for this machine — 14,000 Btu/h under the ASHRAE method and 9,500 Btu/h under the DOE 2017 SACC standard, 32% apart — because SACC accounts for the warm air a portable unit’s own hose arrangement drags back into the room and ASHRAE does not. It changes nothing about the ranking above, which is computed from electrical draw rather than from cooling output. What it changes is whether the appliance you are about to power is the size the box says it is: two units advertised at the same BTU can be a third apart once both are read on the SACC line.

Pricing, ranking and how the site is funded are not questions about this list — they are the same on every page here, and they are set out in full in the price policy and how the money works.
